questions.title: Segments and midpoints
questions.stem: Points A, M, and B lie on one straight line in that order. M is the midpoint of AB. AM = 3x − 2 cm and MB = x + 6 cm.
parts: Find x and the length AB. Explain the equation you use.
A point N lies on segment MB and MN = 3 cm. Find AN and NB. Label the point order on a sketch.
solution: Midpoint means AM = MB, so 3x − 2 = x + 6, giving x = 4. AM = MB = 10 cm and AB = 20 cm.
The order is A–M–N–B. AN = AM + MN = 10 + 3 = 13 cm; NB = MB − MN = 10 − 3 = 7 cm. The lengths total 20 cm.
rubric: AN = 13 cm (1), NB = 7 cm (1), valid addition/subtraction with units (1).
questions.errors: Adding the expressions without using the midpoint; placing N outside MB.

questions.title: Parallel lines and a transversal
questions.stem: In the diagram, lines ℓ and m are parallel. A transversal crosses ℓ at P and m at Q. The marked angle at P is 64°. Angles α and β are the sectors indicated at Q.
parts: Find α and β, naming a geometric relationship for each.
Explain whether knowing the marked 64° angle alone would determine α if the parallel-line condition were removed.
solution: α = 64° by corresponding angles. β = 180° − 64° = 116° by a linear pair (or same-side interior relationships).
No. Without parallelism the lower line can rotate about Q while the upper configuration stays fixed; α can change. The parallel-line hypothesis is essential.
rubric: α = 64° (1); identifies corresponding positions and parallelism (2).
β = 116° (1); uses a 180° linear pair correctly (2).
Says not determined (1) and explains a possible rotation/counterconfiguration (3).
questions.errors: Treating angles as equal because the drawing looks parallel; confusing adjacent and corresponding sectors.

questions.title: Perpendicular directions
questions.stem: A straight ramp rises to the right at 28° above a horizontal line. A vertical line points downward from a point on the ramp. A second ray at that point is perpendicular to the ramp and points downward and to the right.
parts: Draw and label the configuration, including both perpendicular relationships.
Find the smaller angle between the downward vertical ray and the downward-right perpendicular ray. Explain without measuring your sketch.
solution: Draw the ramp up-right, the horizontal right, the vertical down, and the ramp-normal down-right. Vertical is perpendicular to horizontal; the second ray is perpendicular to the ramp.

The ramp makes 62° with the upward vertical. Its perpendicular points 62° below the rightward horizontal, while downward vertical is 90° below horizontal. The difference is 28°. Equivalently, rotating both horizontal and ramp by 90° preserves their 28° angle.
rubric: Correctly orients the two specified rays.
Marks vertical/horizontal and ramp/normal right angles.
Derives the 28° angle from 90° complements or a common rotation.
Reports the smaller angle 28°, not 62° or 152°.
questions.errors: Using the complementary angle or reversing one ray.

questions.title: Equal-distance locations
questions.stem: On a coordinate plane, A = (−2, 1) and B = (6, 1). A point P is equally far from A and B and also lies on the line y = x + 1.
parts: Describe the entire line of points equally far from A and B. Explain its location and direction.
Find P and its exact distance from A. Explain how the two conditions locate P uniquely.
solution: The midpoint of AB is (2,1). AB is horizontal, so its perpendicular bisector is x = 2. Every point on that line is equally far from A and B; points off it are not.

Intersect x = 2 with y = x + 1 to get P = (2,3). PA = √((2 + 2)² + (3 − 1)²) = √20 = 2√5. The vertical line meets the nonvertical line once. An alternative is to equate squared distances, obtain x = 2, and substitute.
questions.errors: Choosing the midpoint as P without checking the other condition; confusing x = 2 and y = 2.

questions.title: Crossing lines
questions.stem: Two full straight lines AB and CD intersect at O. A and B are opposite each other across O, as are C and D. Angle AOC is 37°.
parts: Find angles COB, BOD, and DOA. Draw and label all four sectors.
Explain which angles are vertical and which relationship gives the adjacent angles. Check the sum around O.
solution: AOC and BOD are vertical, as are COB and DOA. Adjacent sectors form linear pairs summing to 180°. The four angles sum to 37 + 143 + 37 + 143 = 360°.
rubric: One point for each correct angle.
A correctly labeled crossing sketch with opposite rays and corresponding sectors.
questions.errors: Calling adjacent angles vertical; making all four equal.

questions.title: Isosceles triangle and extension
questions.stem: Triangle ABC has AB = AC and ∠BAC = 38°. Side BC is extended through C to D.
parts: Find ∠ABC and ∠ACB. State why they are equal.
Find exterior angle ACD and explain its relationship to the interior angles.
solution: The equal sides give equal base angles. Each is (180° − 38°)/2 = 71°.
∠ACD = 180° − 71° = 109°. It also equals the two remote interior angles, 38° + 71°.
rubric: Connects equal sides to equal opposite angles.
Subtracts 38° from 180° (2), divides equally and gives both 71° (2).
Uses a straight angle or the remote-interior sum.
questions.errors: Putting equal angles at the endpoints of the unequal side incorrectly; forgetting the extension direction.

questions.title: A polygon from its angles
questions.stem: Every interior angle of a convex regular polygon measures 150°.
parts: Find the number of sides, showing the angle relationship you use.
Find the number of diagonals drawn from one vertex, and explain how the triangles formed from that vertex check your answer in part (a).
solution: The exterior turning angle is 180° − 150° = 30°. A full turn is 360°, so n = 360/30 = 12. Alternatively solve 150n = 180(n − 2).
There are n − 3 = 9 diagonals from one vertex and n − 2 = 10 triangles. Their angle sum is 10(180°) = 1800°, equal to 12(150°).
rubric: Sets up exterior-turn or interior-sum equation.
Finds 9, excluding the vertex itself and its two neighbors.
questions.errors: Using 360/150; confusing diagonals with triangles.

questions.title: Bisectors in a parallelogram
questions.stem: ABCD is a convex parallelogram with vertices named in order and ∠DAB = 68°. The internal angle bisectors at A and B meet at P inside the parallelogram.
parts: Find ∠APB. Explain why the angle between these two adjacent internal bisectors would have the same measure in any such parallelogram where they meet.
solution: Adjacent parallelogram angles are supplementary: ∠ABC = 112°. Bisecting gives ∠BAP = 34° and ∠ABP = 56°.
In triangle ABP, ∠APB = 180° − 34° − 56° = 90°. In general the original adjacent angles sum to 180°, so their halves sum to 90°, leaving 90° at the intersection.
rubric: Explains half of a supplementary sum is 90° (2), so the remaining triangle angle is 90° regardless of initial angle (2).
questions.errors: Treating the bisectors as equal lengths or halving an angle at the wrong vertex.

questions.title: A hidden bisector
questions.stem: Triangle ABC has AB = AC and ∠BAC = 36°. Point D is strictly between A and C and satisfies BD = BC.
parts: Find ∠ABD and ∠DBC. Decide whether BD bisects ∠ABC and explain using the angles you found.
solution: The base angles of ABC are 72°. Since D lies on AC, ∠BCD = ∠BCA = 72°. In BCD, BD = BC, so the opposite angles BCD and BDC are equal: ∠BDC = 72°.
The remaining angle DBC is 180° − 72° − 72° = 36°. Thus ∠ABD = 72° − 36° = 36°, so BD does bisect ∠ABC. This conclusion follows from the length condition, not from how the drawing looks.
rubric: Transfers BCD = 72° and gets BDC = 72° with correct opposite-side reasoning.
Concludes bisector from the two equal angle measures.
questions.errors: Assuming D is a midpoint or BD a bisector before establishing it; reversing equal-side opposite angles.

questions.title: Which lengths form a triangle?
questions.stem: Two sides of a nondegenerate triangle have lengths 5 cm and 8 cm. The third side has length x cm.
parts: Find the complete range of possible real values of x and explain both endpoints.
If x must be an integer, how many values are possible? Give an example at an excluded endpoint and explain why it fails.
solution: Triangle inequality gives |8 − 5| < x < 8 + 5, so 3 < x < 13. At 3 the shorter segments just span the longest; at 13 the two given sides just span the third. Equality produces a flat, degenerate configuration.
Integers 4 through 12 give 9 possibilities. Either 3 or 13 is excluded because equality collapses the triangle onto a line.
rubric: Gives an endpoint and explains collinearity.
questions.errors: Allowing equality; supplying only the upper bound.

questions.title: A right triangle and its height
questions.stem: Triangle ABC is right-angled at C. AC = 6 cm and BC = 8 cm.
parts: Find AB exactly and identify why it is the hypotenuse.
Find the altitude from C to AB. Use a labeled sketch and explain how you obtain it.
solution: AB is opposite the right angle; AB² = 6² + 8² = 100, so AB = 10 cm.
Area = (1/2)(6)(8) = 24 cm². Using AB as base gives 24 = (1/2)(10)h, hence h = 24/5 cm. A similarity derivation is equally valid.
rubric: Sets up and solves h = 24/5 cm.
Marks altitude perpendicular to AB, not along a leg.
questions.errors: Using a leg as the hypotenuse; assuming a leg is the altitude to AB.

questions.title: Matching triangles
questions.stem: In triangles ABC and DEF, AB = DE = 6 cm, AC = DF = 8 cm, and ∠BAC = ∠EDF = 90°. Also BC = 10 cm.
parts: Explain whether these data guarantee congruence. State the vertex correspondence and find EF.

A second claim says that any two triangles with corresponding side lengths 7 and 9 and a corresponding angle of 50° are congruent, even if that angle is not between the stated sides. Explain why this claim is not generally justified.
solution: SAS applies because the 90° angle is included between the matching 6 and 8 sides. A↔D, B↔E, C↔F, so EF = BC = 10 cm. The 6–8–10 side lengths are consistent with the right angle.

Removing the included-angle requirement can leave SSA data, which do not generally determine a unique triangle. In this separate claim, a side of length 7 opposite 50° and another side of length 9 can produce two triangles: a ray and a circle can meet in two possible third vertices. No numerical construction or sine law is required; a clear SSA ambiguity explanation or sketch suffices.
rubric: Explains that an alternative third vertex can exist, or clearly states SSA is not a general congruence rule.
questions.errors: Using SSA as a general congruence rule; matching vertices by written order alone.

questions.title: Similarity across a triangle
questions.stem: D lies on AB and E lies on AC in triangle ABC, with DE parallel to BC. AD = 6 cm, DB = 3 cm, AE = 8 cm, and BC = 12 cm.
parts: Explain which triangles are similar and find EC.
Find DE and the ratio of the area of triangle ADE to the area of triangle ABC. Explain why the two ratios differ.
solution: ADE and ABC are similar by shared angle A and corresponding angles from DE ∥ BC. AD/AB = 6/9 = 2/3, so AE/AC = 2/3. AC = 12 and EC = 4 cm.
DE = (2/3)(12) = 8 cm. The area ratio is (2/3)² = 4/9 because both a base and its corresponding altitude scale by 2/3.
rubric: Finds 4/9 (1), explains two independent linear factors (2).
questions.errors: Using AD/DB as the scale factor; scaling areas linearly.

questions.title: Right-triangle trigonometry
questions.stem: A 12 m cable runs from level ground to the top of a vertical pole, making an angle of 30° with the ground. In a separate setup, a 10 m cable makes an acute angle θ with level ground.
parts: For the 12 m cable, find the pole height and horizontal ground distance exactly. Explain your trig ratios or special-triangle relationships.
For the separate 10 m cable, express the vertical height and horizontal distance in terms of θ. Explain which side is opposite and which is adjacent to θ.
A separate square has side length 3 cm. Find its diagonal exactly and explain the right-triangle relationship you use.
solution: The cable is the hypotenuse. Height = 12 sin 30° = 6 m. Ground distance = 12 cos 30° = 6√3 m, using the 1:√3:2 ratio.
Height = 10 sin θ m; horizontal distance = 10 cos θ m. The vertical leg is opposite the angle at the ground; the horizontal leg is adjacent. Symbolic expressions are exact and need no calculator.
The diagonal divides the square into two 45°–45°–90° triangles. Its length is 3√2 cm. Equivalently d² = 3² + 3² = 18, so d = √18 = 3√2 cm.
rubric: Height 6 m and horizontal distance 6√3 m (1 each).
Uses the cable as hypotenuse with correct sine/cosine or special-triangle ratios.
10 sin θ and 10 cos θ (1 each).
Explains opposite vertical and adjacent horizontal legs.
questions.errors: Swapping sine and cosine; treating the cable as a leg.

questions.title: A hidden similarity in a right triangle
questions.stem: Triangle ABC is right-angled at C. The perpendicular from C meets hypotenuse AB at D. AD = 4 cm and DB = 9 cm.
parts: Find CD exactly, explaining any similar triangles or other geometric relationships you use.
Find AC and BC exactly. Show a method that checks your values against AB.
solution: Triangles ACD and CBD are similar: both have a right angle at D, and each other acute angle complements the same angle in ABC. Matching sides gives AD/CD = CD/DB, so CD² = 4·9 = 36 and CD = 6 cm. One may also set AC² = 16 + h² and BC² = 81 + h², then AC² + BC² = 169, giving h² = 36.

AB = 13 cm. AC² = AD² + CD² = 16 + 36 = 52, so AC = 2√13 cm. BC² = 81 + 36 = 117, so BC = 3√13 cm. Check: 52 + 117 = 169 = 13². Projection relations AC² = AB·AD and BC² = AB·DB are valid if justified.
rubric: Identifies valid similarity/correspondence or coupled Pythagorean equations.
Checks the squared lengths against AB² = 169.
questions.errors: Assuming altitude bisects the hypotenuse; applying a projection formula to the wrong leg.

questions.title: Central and inscribed angles
questions.stem: A and B lie on a circle with center O. The minor central angle AOB is 124°. C lies on the major arc AB and is distinct from A and B.
parts: Find the minor arc AB measure and ∠ACB. State the relationship between them.
Point D instead lies on the minor arc AB, distinct from A and B. Find ∠ADB and explain which arc it intercepts.
solution: The minor arc measures 124°. C on the major arc sees the minor arc, so ∠ACB = 124°/2 = 62°.
D on the minor arc intercepts the major arc of 360° − 124° = 236°. Thus ∠ADB = 118°. Inscribed angles intercept the arc not containing their vertex.
rubric: Explains central angle equals arc and inscribed angle is half intercepted arc.
questions.errors: Always halving the minor arc regardless of vertex location.

questions.title: A tangent from an exterior point
questions.stem: PT is tangent to a circle with center O at T. OT = 5 cm and OP = 13 cm. The line from P through O meets the circle first at A and then at B.
parts: Find PT exactly and explain the right angle you use.
Find PA and PB. Verify that PT² and PA·PB agree, and distinguish the external secant segment from the whole secant.
solution: A radius to the tangent point is perpendicular to the tangent. PT² = 13² − 5² = 144, so PT = 12 cm.
PA = OP − r = 8 cm; PB = OP + r = 18 cm. PT² = 144 and PA·PB = 8·18 = 144. PA is external; PB is the entire secant from P to its farther intersection.
rubric: Computes and compares both products at 144.
questions.errors: Subtracting the diameter instead of radius; multiplying external by only the internal portion.

questions.title: Intersecting chords
questions.stem: Parts (a) and (b) describe separate circles. In (a), chords AB and CD intersect at X inside a circle, with AX = 3 cm, XB = 8 cm, and CX = 4 cm. In (b), chords EF and GH intersect at Y in another circle; the arc EG not containing F or H is 80°, and the arc FH not containing E or G is 120°.
parts: Find XD in the first circle, stating the segment relationship you use.
Draw the second configuration and find ∠EYG, explaining which arcs determine it. Do not transfer the lengths from part (a) to this separate circle.
solution: Intersecting-chord products give AX·XB = CX·XD. Hence 3·8 = 4·XD and XD = 6 cm.

For chords crossing inside, ∠EYG = (arc EG + arc FH)/2 = (80° + 120°)/2 = 100°. These are the arcs intercepted by the angle and its vertical angle. The circles are separate, so the first part imposes no length restrictions on the second.
rubric: Uses the two parts of each same chord: 3·8 = 4·XD.
Sketches the second circle and selects EG and FH, not adjacent arcs.
questions.errors: Using half a difference for an interior intersection; multiplying segments on different chords.

questions.title: A cyclic quadrilateral
questions.stem: A, B, C, and D occur in that order on one circle. In quadrilateral ABCD, ∠DAB = 3x + 10° and ∠BCD = 5x − 6°. Also ∠ABC = 110°. Side CD is extended through D to E.
parts: Find x and all four interior angles of ABCD.
Find ∠ADE and explain why it equals one of the opposite interior angles.
solution: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: (3x + 10) + (5x − 6) = 180, so x = 22. A = 76°, C = 104°, B = 110°, and D = 70°.
∠ADE = 180° − 70° = 110°, equal to ∠ABC. The exterior angle is supplementary to D, and so is B; therefore they are equal.
rubric: Sets opposite angles to sum to 180°.
A and C correct (1 each); D = 70° with B = 110° retained (1).
Connects the exterior supplement and the opposite interior supplement.
questions.errors: Assuming adjacent cyclic angles are supplementary; extending the wrong side.

questions.title: A chord controls an arc
questions.stem: A circle has radius 10 cm. Chord AB has length 12 cm. M is the midpoint of AB, and O is the center.
parts: Find OM and explain why triangle OMA is right-angled.
Let φ = ∠AOM be acute. Express the minor central angle AOB and the length of the minor arc AB exactly using inverse trigonometry. State the angle units you use for arc length.
solution: OA = OB and AM = MB, so the center-to-midpoint line is perpendicular to the chord (by symmetry or congruent triangles). AM = 6; OM = √(100 − 36) = 8 cm.

sin φ = 6/10 = 3/5 (or tan φ = 3/4). The minor central angle is 2 arcsin(3/5) radians, and arc length is rθ = 20 arcsin(3/5) cm. Equivalent forms using arctan(3/4) or arccos(4/5) earn full credit. No decimal evaluation is required.
rubric: Explains OM perpendicular to AB and AM = 6.
Obtains φ from a correct ratio.
Doubles φ for the minor central angle.
Uses radians and rθ for 20 arcsin(3/5) cm (1 each).
questions.errors: Using the chord as arc length; forgetting to double the half-angle; substituting degrees directly into rθ.

questions.title: A cut-out rectangle
questions.stem: A rectangle is 12 cm wide and 9 cm high. A 4 cm by 3 cm rectangle is removed from its upper-right corner.
parts: Sketch the remaining L-shaped region and find its area.
Find the perimeter of the remaining region. Explain why subtracting the cut-out perimeter from the original perimeter would be wrong.
solution: Original area = 12·9 = 108 cm². Remove 4·3 = 12 cm², leaving 96 cm².
The new boundary lengths are 12, 6, 4, 3, 8, and 9 cm, totaling 42 cm. Removing the corner replaces boundary lengths 4 and 3 by new lengths 4 and 3; the perimeter remains 2(12 + 9) = 42 cm.
rubric: Sketches a corner removal with consistent dimensions.
Explains the replaced boundary lengths; rejects subtracting all four cut-out edges.
questions.errors: Mixing area and perimeter; counting interior edges as boundary.

questions.title: Two diagonals and a height
questions.stem: A rhombus has perpendicular diagonals of lengths 10 cm and 24 cm. A separate parallelogram has base 13 cm and perpendicular height 8 cm.
parts: Find the rhombus area by decomposing it into triangles. Find its side length as a check on your sketch.
Find the parallelogram area. A learner uses a sloping side of length 10 cm as the height instead. Explain the error.
solution: The diagonals bisect each other. Four right triangles have legs 5 and 12 cm, each area 30 cm²; total area is 120 cm². The side is √(5² + 12²) = 13 cm.
Area = base times perpendicular height = 13·8 = 104 cm². A sloping side is not the perpendicular distance between parallel bases, so 13·10 is not justified.
rubric: Uses half-diagonals 5 and 12 and four triangles.
Explains why sloping length cannot replace perpendicular height.
questions.errors: Using full diagonals as triangle legs; confusing sloping and perpendicular height.

questions.title: A circular segment
questions.stem: In a circle of radius 6 cm, the minor central angle AOB is 120°. The minor circular segment is the region between chord AB and its minor arc.
parts: Find the area of minor sector AOB.
Find the area of the minor circular segment exactly. Show how you find the triangle area without the laws of sines or cosines.
solution: Bisect the 120° angle and drop a perpendicular from O to AB. Each right triangle has hypotenuse 6 and central angle 60°, giving half-base 3√3 and height 3. Triangle AOB has area (1/2)(6√3)(3) = 9√3 cm². Segment area = 12π − 9√3 cm². Using (1/2)r² sin 120° is valid basic trig if the height relationship is explained.
rubric: Uses one third of the circle.
Draws/identifies the perpendicular that bisects the isosceles triangle.
Gets 9√3 from a correct base and height or justified trig height.
questions.errors: Confusing sector with segment; subtracting the wrong triangle.

questions.title: Recover a triangle from its inner strip
questions.stem: D lies on AB and E on AC in triangle ABC, with DE parallel to BC. AD:DB = 2:1. The area of quadrilateral DBCE is 45 cm².
parts: Find the areas of triangle ABC and triangle ADE. Explain how the given length ratio determines an area ratio.
A second segment parallel to BC cuts off a triangle at A whose area is half the area of ABC. Find its side-length scale factor relative to ABC, and explain why that factor is not 1/2.
solution: AD/AB = 2/3, so [ADE]/[ABC] = 4/9. The strip DBCE is 5/9 of the whole. Therefore [ABC] = 45·9/5 = 81 cm² and [ADE] = 36 cm².
If the length factor is k, its area factor is k². Set k² = 1/2; positive k = 1/√2 = √2/2. A factor 1/2 in length would give 1/4 in area.
rubric: Squares to 4/9 and uses strip fraction 5/9 (1 each).
Finds √2/2 and explains why linear half is incorrect.
questions.errors: Using 2:1 directly as small-to-whole; treating the strip as half the whole.

questions.title: A prism and a cylinder
questions.stem: A right triangular prism has a right-triangle base with perpendicular legs 6 cm and 8 cm, and length 10 cm. A separate cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 5 cm.
parts: Find the prism volume, showing its base area.
Find the cylinder volume. Explain the common geometric structure in the two volume calculations and state the units.
solution: Triangular base area = (1/2)(6)(8) = 24 cm². Volume = 24·10 = 240 cm³.
Circular base area = π·3² = 9π cm². Volume = 9π·5 = 45π cm³. Both use constant cross-sectional/base area times perpendicular length or height, producing cubic units.
rubric: Multiplies by prism length (1), finds 240 cm³ (2).
Explains base area times height and cubic units.
questions.errors: Omitting the triangle factor 1/2; multiplying perimeter by height for volume.

questions.title: A tank with a conical roof
questions.stem: A closed solid consists of a right circular cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm, topped by a right circular cone of the same radius and perpendicular height 4 cm. Their circular joining faces coincide, and their interiors do not overlap.
parts: Find the total solid volume. Label the two heights in a sketch.
A geometrically similar solid has every length doubled. Find its volume and the ratio of new volume to original volume. Explain the scale factor.
solution: Cylinder: π·3²·8 = 72π. Cone: (1/3)π·3²·4 = 12π. Total = 84π cm³. The cone height is its perpendicular 4 cm height, not the sloping edge.
Doubling three linear dimensions multiplies volume by 2³ = 8, so new volume = 672π cm³. New:original volume = 8:1.
rubric: Sketch distinguishes cylinder height 8 and cone height 4.
Uses factor 8 and explains cubic scaling.
questions.errors: Using total height for each component; forgetting cone factor 1/3; doubling volume instead of cubing scale.

questions.title: Material left after drilling
questions.stem: In (a), a cube has side length 10 cm. A cylindrical hole of radius 2 cm is drilled straight through its center, perpendicular to two opposite faces. No material outside the cylinder is removed. Part (b) concerns a separate hollow sphere.
parts: Find the volume of material remaining in the cube. Draw or describe the removed cylinder dimensions.
A hollow sphere has outer radius 5 cm and concentric inner radius 3 cm. Find its material volume exactly. Explain why inserting the wall thickness as the radius of a solid sphere would be incorrect.
solution: Cube volume = 1000 cm³. The hole is a radius-2, height-10 cylinder, of volume 40π cm³. Remaining volume is 1000 − 40π cm³.
Material volume = (4/3)π(5³ − 3³) = (4/3)π(98) = 392π/3 cm³. A solid sphere of radius 5 − 3 = 2 cm is a different region. Cubing the difference is not the same as subtracting the cubes.
rubric: Subtracts full sphere volumes with the correct 4π/3 factor.
Explains why a radius-2 solid sphere is not the shell.
questions.errors: Using diameter as radius; subtracting only an opening area; cubing wall thickness instead of subtracting two sphere volumes.

questions.title: An open rectangular box
questions.stem: A thin-walled rectangular box has internal and external dimensions treated as identical: length 8 cm, width 5 cm, height 3 cm. It has a bottom and four side walls, but no lid. Ignore wall thickness and count only one side of each material panel.
parts: Sketch a possible net, label its panels, and find the total panel area.
Find the extra area needed to add a lid. Explain how the no-lid instruction changes the closed-box surface-area calculation.
solution: The net has one 8×5 bottom, two 8×3 walls, and two 5×3 walls. Area = 40 + 48 + 30 = 118 cm².
A lid adds 8·5 = 40 cm². Closed-box area is 158 cm², so the open-box area is 158 − 40 = 118 cm². Counting both physical sides would be a different question.
rubric: Shows one bottom and four suitably joined side panels.
Explains omission of exactly one base; closed total 158 cm².
questions.errors: Including a lid; counting a face twice; reporting cubic units.

questions.title: Cylinder net and missing end
questions.stem: A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. First consider the closed cylinder, then the same cylinder with its upper circular face removed. Ignore thickness and count each surface once.
parts: Sketch the net of the closed cylinder. Label the rectangle dimensions and find both its lateral area and total surface area.
Find the surface area after the upper face is removed. Explain precisely which area disappears.
A separate sphere has radius 3 cm. Find its surface area and explain why using the area of one circular disk would not answer this question.
solution: The curved surface unwraps into a rectangle of width 2πr = 6π cm and height 10 cm. Lateral area = 60π cm². The two disks add 18π, giving total surface area 78π cm².
One disk has area 9π cm². Removing the upper face leaves 60π + 9π = 69π cm². The bottom disk and the full curved wall remain.
Sphere surface area = 4πr² = 36π cm². A disk area πr² = 9π describes a flat cross-section, not the entire curved spherical surface.
rubric: Labels rectangle 6π by 10 and includes two radius-3 disks.
Gets 69π cm² and describes remaining surfaces.
Distinguishes one flat disk from the whole sphere surface.
questions.errors: Unwrapping to diameter by height; confusing lateral area and total area; confusing a sphere with a disk.

questions.title: Exposed surfaces of a joined solid
questions.stem: A closed solid consists of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm, topped by a cone of the same radius and perpendicular height 4 cm. Their circular joining faces coincide. Only the exterior surface is to be painted; include the bottom disk.
parts: Find the cone slant height and the total exterior area to be painted. Explain which surfaces are hidden.
A model has all lengths multiplied by 3. Find its exterior area. Explain why simply adding the full surface areas of the original cone and cylinder would overcount.
solution: Cone slant height is √(3² + 4²) = 5 cm. Exposed areas: cylinder wall 2π·3·8 = 48π; cone wall π·3·5 = 15π; bottom disk 9π. Total = 72π cm². Both coincident joining disks are internal and excluded.
Area scales by 3² = 9, so model exterior area = 648π cm². Full cone plus full cylinder areas count the common circular interface twice, overcounting by 2πr² = 18π cm² for the original solid.
rubric: Uses right triangle to get slant height 5.
Finds 48π cylinder wall and 15π cone wall (1 each).
Includes only bottom disk and totals 72π.
Explains two hidden disks and overcount 18π cm².
questions.errors: Using perpendicular cone height in lateral area; counting the hidden joining disks; cubing the area scale.

references.A10.2: AoPS Vol. 1, §10.2, Classification and Measurement, pp. 84–86.
references.A10.3: AoPS Vol. 1, §10.3, Angles and Parallel Lines, p. 86.
